slides.title: Holy Priesthood
body: TALMIDO  /  CHAPTER 6

Christ our High Priest
and our call to serve
Sixth-grade Sunday school
slides.notes: Suggested time: 10–12 minutes. Ask: Who helps people know God in our parish? Accept several ministries, then introduce the particular role of ordained priests.

slides.title: Christ our High Priest
body:
Jesus offered Himself on the Cross
to reunite us with God.

After His Resurrection, Jesus asked Peter
to care for His people.
slides.notes: Jesus offered Himself willingly on the Cross for our sins. His sacrifice restores communion with God. Introduce priest as someone set apart to serve God and His people. Connect service to John 21:15–17: the risen Jesus calls Peter to care for His flock.

slides.title: Priests in the Old Testament
body: Aaron

God called Aaron to serve
as high priest.
Set apart for service

Priests offered sacrifices,
taught God’s law, and prayed
on behalf of the people.
Priesthood continued through Aaron’s family.
slides.notes: God instructed Moses to anoint Aaron. After Aaron, his son Eleazar became high priest. The lesson describes priesthood continuing through this lineage and within the tribe of Levi. Priests offered sacrifices, taught the law, maintained the sanctuary, and interceded for people. Intercede means pray on someone else’s behalf.

slides.title: Melchizedek and Christ
body:
King of Salem
Priest of God Most High

He offered bread and wine
and blessed Abraham.

The lesson connects him with
Christ’s everlasting priesthood.
slides.notes: Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He offered bread and wine and blessed Abraham. The curriculum connects him with Christ’s everlasting priesthood. References: Genesis 14:18–20, Hebrews 7:2–3 and Psalm 109:1–4 using OSB numbering. Ask students to notice bread and wine in the supplied icon. Image source: icon reproduced on printed page 35 of the user-supplied curriculum.

slides.title: Ordained ministry in the Church
body:
Christ entrusted His work
to the Apostles.

Through the Holy Spirit and the laying on of hands,
the Church continues ordained ministry.
In the Eucharist, Christ acts through the priest.
slides.notes: Christ entrusted His priestly work to the Apostles. The lesson describes the Holy Spirit’s guidance and laying on of hands for ordination. Bishops, priests, and deacons have particular ministries. Explain the priest’s role in the Eucharist without equating the human priest with Christ: Christ Himself acts through the priest. The Kukiliyon remembers priesthood and the Apostles spreading it throughout creation.

slides.title: The calling of every Christian
body: A royal priesthood

Every Christian has a part in serving God
and caring for His creation.
We share God’s wonderful deeds and His love.
1 Peter 2:9
slides.notes: Read 1 Peter 2:9 from the Orthodox Study Bible if available. The lesson describes all the faithful as a royal priesthood with responsibilities in creation. The general calling belongs to men and women. Explain that this shared calling supports, but does not erase, the distinct calling of ordained ministers.

slides.title: Our shared calling and particular ministries
body: All Christians

Follow God’s will.
Care for creation.
Share His love with others.
Ordained ministers

Receive a particular calling.
Serve through ordination.
Help the community worship
and draw near to Christ.
slides.notes: Use this comparison to check the main lesson goal. All Christians serve God; ordained ministers have a particular ministry through ordination. Both belong to the life of the Church. Ask: How might a student support the parish’s ministry? Possible examples: pray, help, welcome someone, care for creation. These are teaching applications, not quoted textbook examples.

slides.title: Service in everyday life
body:
A new student arrives at Sunday school
and does not know anyone.
How could you show Christ’s love?
Name one action you could take this week.
slides.notes: Suggested discussion: 1 minute. This classroom scenario applies the lesson’s call to service; it is newly written, not a textbook event. Possible answers: introduce yourself, invite the student to sit with you, explain where to find the lesson, or include them in an activity. Do not ask students to disclose private experiences.

slides.title: Chapter 6 quick quiz
body: 1. Who became the high priest of the Tabernacle?
2. Why does the lesson call Christ our High Priest?

3. Does the call to serve God belong only to
    ordained priests? Explain your answer.
slides.notes: Allow students to answer before moving to the final slide. Q1 is recall; Q2 checks the Christ-centered meaning of priesthood; Q3 checks the distinction between the general and particular call. These are newly written curriculum-based questions.

slides.title: Answers and one idea to remember
body: 1. Aaron

2. Christ offered Himself on the Cross
    to reunite us with God.

3. All Christians serve God. Ordained ministers
    have a particular calling within the Church.
Christ is our High Priest. We all have a call to serve.
slides.notes: Suggested answers: 1 Aaron. 2 Jesus offered Himself as the perfect sacrifice on the Cross and reunited us with God. 3 No. All Christians share a calling to serve God and care for His creation; ordained ministers have particular responsibilities. Accept equivalent meaning. Exit prompt: ask each student to name one concrete act of service.

slides.title: The Living Sacrifice
body: Chapter 7 explains what happens during the Holy Qurbana and why it matters. The prayers and actions help us understand our relationship with Christ and with one another.
We will follow the service step by step, explain unfamiliar words, and connect what happens in church with how we live during the week.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: The big picture: two parts of worship
body: The first part is the Pre-Anaphora, also called the Liturgy of the Word. We hear hymns, prayers, and Bible readings that prepare us for the Eucharistic offering.
The second part is the Anaphora, also called the Liturgy of the Upper Room. It centers on the Eucharist and our participation in Christ’s Body and Blood.
The main liturgy used in the Malankara Church is the Liturgy of St. James. The lesson connects our worship today with the worship of the Apostles.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Who were the catechumens?
body: Catechumens are people learning the Christian faith in preparation for baptism. This is why the first part also has the name Liturgy of the Catechumens.
Historically, catechumens stayed for the hymns and Scripture readings. They left before the Anaphora, while the baptized faithful continued with the Eucharistic worship.
These names help us remember the movement of the service: we hear God’s Word, then enter the Eucharistic offering.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 1. The curtain opens and the hymn begins
body: As the curtain opens, the priest asks St. Mary, the mother of Jesus, and St. John the Baptist to intercede for us. Intercede means to pray on someone else’s behalf.
Then we sing the Maneesa, also called Ma’nitho, of St. Severus. The textbook describes this hymn as a summary of our Orthodox faith and of God’s love for us.
The unfamiliar name belongs to a familiar action: the Church begins by singing its faith together.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 2. The procession tells a Gospel story
body: A server carries a candle ahead of the priest. The candle bearer represents John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus. This is why John is called the Forerunner.
The priest represents Christ. Servers carrying maravasas accompany the procession around the altar. Maravasas are the ceremonial metal fans used in worship.
The order helps us remember the Gospel: John prepares the way, then Christ comes. Ask: Why does the candle bearer walk ahead?
slides.notes: The user-supplied teaching reference also explains the maravasas as representing the angels around God’s throne. You may point this out when discussing the procession.

slides.title: 3. The Trisagion: a prayer of holiness
body: The Trisagion is the prayer beginning “Holy art Thou, O God.” Its name means “three times holy.” The prayer praises God’s holiness and asks for mercy.
The textbook shares a Church tradition about Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus hearing heavenly praise while carrying Jesus’ body. They added the words about Christ’s crucifixion.
This is why the lesson calls the prayer a combination of angelic and human praise. This account is a liturgical tradition, rather than a scene narrated in the Gospels.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 4. The Bible readings, in order
body: First comes a reading from Acts or the Catholic Epistles, read from the northern step of the sanctuary. Catholic Epistles means the general letters of James, Peter, John, and Jude.
Second comes a reading from St. Paul’s letters, from the southern step. Then the priest reads the Gospel from the center of the Madbaha, the altar area.
Here, “catholic” means universal. The name describes the general letters and does not mean that the reading comes from the Roman Catholic Church.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 5. Listening and the sermon
body: Before the Gospel, the deacon calls everyone to attend with stillness, fear, and purity. In plain language: be quiet, be reverent, and give God your attention.
The sermon explains the Scripture and helps us live it. The lesson places it after the Gospel, while noting that some parishes move it later for practical reasons.
The textbook compares Scripture to food for the soul. Ask: If a reading teaches us to love our neighbor, what could that change about tomorrow at school?
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 6. Prayers for mercy and the incense
body: Promion, Husoyo, and Sedro are names for prayers in this part of the service. The priest first asks God’s mercy for himself, then for the faithful, both living and departed.
The priest blesses the censer while proclaiming the holiness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The censer is the vessel that holds the burning incense.
As the fragrant smoke rises, it helps us picture our prayers rising to God. The lesson connects this with incense in Scripture and with the prayers of the saints.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 7. The Creed: the faith we share
body: The Nicene Creed is the Church’s statement of faith. We confess what we believe about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and about the Church’s life and hope.
The textbook connects this shared confession with baptism. Historically, those preparing for baptism left at this point, before the Anaphora.
The Creed helps us recognize that we worship as one community sharing the same faith, even though we bring different needs and experiences.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 8. The Kiss of Peace begins the Anaphora
body: The peace begins at the altar and passes through the ministers to the congregation. Each person shares it with others until it reaches the whole church.
The lesson compares this with Christ giving His peace to the Apostles, who shared it with their disciples and with the world. The peace comes from God.
It also asks something of us: sincere reconciliation. Jesus teaches us to make peace with another person before bringing our offering. An outward gesture should express an inward intention.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 9. The veil and the call to attention
body: The Shoshappa, or Shushefo, is the cloth covering the paten and chalice. The paten holds the bread and the chalice holds the wine. The veil also recalls the stone at Christ’s tomb.
As the veil is lifted, the deacon calls the faithful to stand with reverence, purity, love, and true faith. Our attention turns toward God and thanksgiving.
The priest gives a Trinitarian blessing, a blessing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “Trinitarian” refers to the Holy Trinity.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 10. Joining the praise of heaven
body: The priest calls us to lift our thoughts and hearts toward Christ. The service asks for the attention of our whole person, including our mind and heart.
We sing the Sanctus, the hymn of “Holy, Holy, Holy.” The lesson connects this with the praise of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:3. Seraphim are heavenly beings who worship God.
The meaning is that the worship of the Church on earth joins the worship of heaven. We belong to a much larger communion than the people we can see around us.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 11. The Words of Institution
body: The Words of Institution recall Christ establishing the Eucharist at the Mystical Supper. We hear the account of His giving the bread and wine as His Body and Blood.
The Church believes that in Holy Communion we receive the real Body and Blood of Christ. This belief explains the reverence with which we approach the Mysteries.
We remember His death, confess His Resurrection, and await His coming again. The service brings our attention to the saving work through which Christ gives us life.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 12. The Epiclesis: calling on the Spirit
body: Epiclesis means invocation or calling upon. Here the priest calls upon the Holy Spirit to descend upon the gifts. The lesson describes their consecration as Christ’s Body and Blood.
The congregation responds with “Kurielaison,” meaning “Lord, have mercy.” Even while the priest prays quietly, the people participate with attention and prayer.
Consecration means making holy or setting apart for God. In this part of the service, the word refers to the Holy Spirit’s work in the Eucharistic gifts.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 13. The Diptychs: prayers for the living
body: Diptychs, also called Thubden, are the prayers of remembrance and intercession. Having drawn near to God, we bring the needs of the whole Church before Him.
The first remembers living Church leaders. The second remembers the sick, the suffering, and people who have requested prayer. The third remembers those in civil authority.
The congregation continues to respond, “Lord, have mercy.” Sitting during these prayers does not mean our participation has stopped.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: The Diptychs: saints and the departed
body: The fourth Diptych commemorates St. Mary and the saints. The fifth remembers the teachers, or doctors, of the Church who preserved and handed down the faith.
The sixth remembers all the faithful departed, including our loved ones who have died. “Departed” means those who have passed from this life.
This answers an important chapter question: the Holy Qurbana is the worship of a communion that includes the living and the departed.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 14. The Fraction and the Lord’s Prayer
body: During the Fraction, the curtain closes and the priest breaks the consecrated Bread. The lesson connects this solemn action with Christ’s death and preparation for burial.
When the curtain opens again, we pray the Lord’s Prayer. Calling God “Our Father” expresses the closeness with Him that Christ restores.
The request for daily bread also prepares us to receive Christ, the Bread of Life. We depend on God for our nourishment and life.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 15. The Elevation and Holy Communion
body: The priest lifts the paten and chalice containing the Holy Mysteries. This is the Elevation. The congregation glorifies the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as holy.
The priest then brings the Mysteries to the people for Communion. We receive Christ with reverence because of who He is and the holiness of His gift.
The chapter calls us to approach with a repentant heart. Holy Confession and guidance from our spiritual father help us prepare to receive.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: What changes after we leave church?
body: The Holy Qurbana gives us a foundation for everyday life. The love and peace we receive should shape how we speak, forgive, and care for other people.
For example, someone who shares the Kiss of Peace on Sunday can practice that peace by welcoming a lonely classmate on Monday or making amends after an argument.
As we grow, familiar prayers can take on deeper meaning. Ask: Which part of the service will you pay closer attention to next Sunday, and why?
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Chapter 7: questions to talk through
body: 1. What are the two main parts of the Holy Qurbana? Why is the first part also called the Liturgy of the Catechumens?
2. Why does the candle bearer go ahead of the priest? What should sharing the Kiss of Peace mean in our relationships?
3. What is the Epiclesis? How do the Diptychs show that our worship includes both the living and the departed?
slides.notes: Give students time to explain in their own words. These are curriculum-based practice questions, not a request for exact memorized wording.

slides.title: Chapter 7: answers with explanations
body: 1. Pre-Anaphora and Anaphora. Catechumens are people preparing for baptism, who historically stayed for the first part and left before the Eucharistic offering.
2. The candle bearer represents John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ. The Kiss of Peace calls us to share God’s peace and seek sincere reconciliation.
3. The Epiclesis invokes the Holy Spirit. The Diptychs remember living people, the saints, and the faithful departed, expressing the communion of the whole Church.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Holy Confession
body: Chapter 8 explains how we return to God when sin has wounded our relationship with Him. The Church presents Confession as a sacrament of healing.
We will look at God’s welcome, the priest’s role, how to prepare, and why repentance includes the way we treat other people.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: The big picture: sin and healing
body: The chapter compares sin with spiritual sickness. When we choose sin, we turn away from God and damage our communion, or shared life, with Him.
Confession helps us return. We acknowledge our sins, repent, and receive God’s forgiveness through the ministry He has entrusted to the Church.
The comparison with sickness helps explain our need for care and healing. It does not mean that physical illness is proof that a person has sinned.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: The prodigal son: why the story matters
body: The prodigal son leaves his father and becomes separated from his family’s love and life. The chapter uses his loneliness as a picture of what sin does to our communion with God.
When the son turns back, his father welcomes him. The father’s response shows the love with which God receives those who return in repentance.
The important movement is leaving, recognizing our need, and returning. Ask: What does the father’s welcome teach us about approaching God after doing wrong?
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Repentance means turning back
body: Repentance includes recognizing that we have done wrong, being sincerely sorry, and choosing to turn toward God again. It changes the direction we want our life to take.
The chapter also recalls the lost sheep and the joy in heaven when a sinner repents. God wants our return and restoration, so we can approach Him with hope.
Feeling embarrassed can make us want to hide. Repentance moves us toward honesty, help, and a renewed relationship with God.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Why do we confess before a priest?
body: We confess to God in the presence of the priest. God is the source of forgiveness. The priest witnesses our confession, guides us, and ministers God’s forgiveness.
The chapter compares the priest’s role with a doctor’s care. A doctor helps a sick person seek healing, and a spiritual father helps us recognize and overcome patterns of sin.
Personal prayer remains important. Sacramental Confession is the particular way the Church gives us this ministry of guidance and absolution.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Where does the priest’s authority come from?
body: The chapter points to John 20:23, where Christ gives the Apostles authority concerning the forgiveness of sins. Their ministry comes from Christ.
Through ordination, with the laying on of hands, this ministry continues through bishops and priests. The lesson calls this apostolic succession.
Absolution means the forgiveness of sins ministered in Confession. The priest serves through the authority Christ gives His Church, rather than through personal power.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Feeling nervous about Confession
body: It is natural to feel nervous when speaking honestly about something shameful or painful. The textbook explains that the priest is there to listen, guide, and pray for forgiveness.
Getting to know a trusted spiritual father can make it easier to seek help consistently. The chapter recommends a relationship with a priest who knows and can guide you.
You can tell the priest that you are nervous or unsure how to begin. Asking for help is a sensible first step.
slides.notes: Keep classroom discussion general. Do not invite children to disclose their sins to the teacher or class.

slides.title: 1. Preparation: examine yourself
body: Before Confession, take time to think honestly about your thoughts, words, and actions. Notice where you have turned away from God or hurt other people.
The textbook suggests writing private reminders so you do not forget what you want to confess. The purpose is honest reflection, not producing impressive words.
A useful private question is: What happened, what part was my responsibility, and what do I need help to change?
slides.notes: Do not collect or read students’ private lists. The final question is a teaching aid, not a quotation from the curriculum.

slides.title: 2. Preparation: sincere repentance
body: Confession asks us to be honest and genuinely sorry. If we hide the very thing for which we need help, it becomes harder to receive useful guidance.
The textbook suggests prayerful reflection on the penitential Psalms. These prayers help us express sorrow, ask for mercy, and trust in God.
The goal is to speak truthfully to God and seek healing. We do not need to pretend that we already have everything under control.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: 3. Preparation: a real intention to change
body: Repentance includes an intention to resist the sin and work with our priest on ways to overcome it. We take practical steps instead of simply repeating the same apology.
For example, a person who spreads a rumor can stop repeating it, correct the false statement, and apologize to the person harmed. This example applies the lesson to school life.
Ask: What would show that this person really wants to change? Look for actions that repair harm and prevent it from happening again.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: What if I make the same mistake again?
body: The chapter asks whether we should confess when we know we might sin again. Our struggle is a reason to seek help and keep repenting, rather than give up.
A sincere intention to change does not mean claiming we will never struggle again. We return honestly, accept guidance, and continue making an effort.
We should also avoid planning to do wrong on the assumption that we can confess afterward. Repentance includes a real desire to turn away from the sin.
slides.notes: This slide explains the textbook’s reflection question in light of its instructions to repent sincerely and work with the priest.

slides.title: Forgiving and making peace
body: The chapter connects asking God’s forgiveness with forgiving other people. It also calls us to seek forgiveness from those we have hurt and work toward reconciliation.
This is why the Kiss of Peace matters in the Holy Qurbana. We express a willingness to live in peace with others while approaching God together.
Forgiveness can take effort. If someone is hurting or threatening you, seek help from a trusted adult. Forgiving does not require hiding harm or remaining unsafe.
slides.notes: The last paragraph is age-appropriate pastoral application, rather than a quotation from the textbook.

slides.title: How often? What about Holy Communion?
body: The textbook mentions recommendations about regular Confession, then tells us to discuss frequency with our priest. Our spiritual father helps guide our particular preparation.
Confession also renews our baptismal commitment to turn away from evil and follow Christ. The Christian life includes returning and growing throughout our lives.
Chapter 7 connects Confession with preparing for Holy Communion. Repentance and reconciliation help us approach the Holy Mysteries with an attentive heart.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Chapter 8: questions to talk through
body: 1. Why does the chapter describe Confession as healing? What does the prodigal son’s father teach us about God?
2. If God forgives us, what is the priest’s role? What does apostolic succession mean in this lesson?
3. Name the main steps of preparation. Should someone who struggles with the same sin give up on Confession? Explain why.
slides.notes: Accept explanations in the student’s own words. Keep examples fictional and never ask for personal confessions.

slides.title: Chapter 8: answers with explanations
body: 1. Sin wounds our communion with God, and Confession helps restore it. The father welcomes his returning son, showing God’s love toward those who repent.
2. The priest witnesses, guides, and ministers forgiveness. Apostolic succession connects his ordained ministry through the bishops and Apostles to Christ.
3. Examine yourself, repent honestly, and intend to change while seeking reconciliation. Keep seeking help when you struggle, with a sincere desire to grow.
slides.notes: Read the explanation together. Invite the student to explain the main idea in their own words before continuing.

slides.title: Anointing of the Sick
body: TALMIDO / CHAPTER 9
Christ cares for the whole person
Prayer, healing, and the love of the Church.
slides.notes: Allow 12–15 minutes. Be sensitive to students with sick or grieving family members. Do not promise that a sacrament guarantees physical recovery.

slides.title: God does not abandon us in suffering
body: We live in a world marked by suffering.
Illness is not proof of a person’s sin.
Christ meets us with compassion.
slides.notes: Avoid blaming a sick person. The curriculum places suffering in the fallen condition of the world and presents Christ as healer. Students may need reassurance that illness is not their fault.

slides.title: Healing is more than physical recovery
body: We bring body and soul before God.
We seek strength, peace, and healing.
The Church supports the whole person.
slides.notes: The lesson includes physical, spiritual, mental, and emotional needs. God’s care is present even when an illness continues. Encourage medical care alongside prayer.

slides.title: A sacrament for those who are sick
body: Holy Unction is another name for this sacrament.
It is not only for the moment of death.
It may be received again when needed.
slides.notes: Explain unction as anointing. Refer students and families to their priest for pastoral guidance. Avoid treating the rite as a last resort or as a replacement for treatment.

slides.title: Prayer and anointing
body: Scripture, hymns, and prayers are offered.
The priest prays and anoints with holy oil.
James 5:14–15 connects prayer and anointing.
slides.notes: The curriculum describes the priest placing a hand on the head, an opportunity for confession, and anointing the forehead and chest with olive oil (zythe). This is distinct from Holy Chrism. Paraphrase Scripture rather than inventing a quotation.

slides.title: The Good Samaritan: compassion in action
body: He sees the wounded man.
He stops and cares for him.
Love becomes practical help.
slides.notes: Retell the Good Samaritan briefly. The curriculum’s Church interpretation sees Christ in the compassionate Samaritan and the Church in the inn. Identify this as a spiritual reading of the parable. Image: Good Samaritan icon reproduced in the curriculum, printed p. 54.

slides.title: We can care for people who are sick
body: Pray for them.
Offer company and encouragement.
Support the care they need.
slides.notes: Age-appropriate actions include a card, a kind message, or a family-approved visit. Respect rest, privacy, and health precautions. Prayer complements medical care.

slides.title: How could you help?
body: A friend is away from school because of illness.
They feel lonely and left out.
Name one kind action you could take.
slides.notes: New classroom application. Examples: send a message, share class notes, make a card, or include them remotely when appropriate. Do not speculate about the illness or demand private details.

slides.title: Chapter 9 quick quiz
body: 1. What is another name for this sacrament?
2. Is it only for someone near death?
3. Name one way we can care for the sick.
slides.notes: Allow students to answer before advancing. These are newly written curriculum-based practice questions.

slides.title: Answers and one idea to remember
body: 1. Holy Unction.
2. No. It is for the sick and may be repeated.
3. Pray, encourage, visit appropriately, or help.
Christ’s compassion calls us to care.
slides.notes: Accept suitable practical examples. Reaffirm that prayer and medical care belong together and that ongoing illness does not mean weak faith.

slides.title: A Christian Home
body: TALMIDO / CHAPTER 10
A home that welcomes Christ
Prayer, love, and faith in everyday life.
slides.notes: Allow 12–15 minutes. Welcome different family structures and living situations. A Christian home is defined by its life in Christ, not its size, wealth, or furnishings.

slides.title: The home extends the life of the Church
body: Faith is lived beyond the church building.
Families pray and give thanks together.
Daily love makes our faith visible.
slides.notes: The lesson calls the family the smallest unit of the Church. Emphasize that children can practice faith through kindness and prayer in varied household circumstances.

slides.title: Why bless a home?
body: We dedicate our home and life to God.
We ask for His presence and protection.
We renew our commitment to live in His love.
slides.notes: A house blessing is not a substitute for loving conduct. Explain annual renewal as part of the curriculum’s practice, with local arrangements guided by the parish priest.

slides.title: Prepare simply and prayerfully
body: Make space for prayer.
Prepare the items the priest requests.
Prayer and charity matter more than luxury.
slides.notes: The curriculum describes a table with white cloth, water, candles, cross, and incense, with room to pray facing east. Coordinate actual arrangements with the priest. The lesson emphasizes spiritual preparation, fasting, prayer, and charity.

slides.title: What happens at a house blessing?
body: The household gathers for prayer.
We hear the Gospel and share the Church’s faith.
Blessed water and the cross mark the home.
slides.notes: The order includes Kauma, hymns, Gospel, prayers, blessing and sprinkling water, marking doorposts with the cross, Creed, incense, and benediction. Present the overall meaning instead of a rigid how-to ritual.

slides.title: Zacchaeus welcomes Jesus
body: Zacchaeus wants to see Jesus.
Jesus comes to his home.
A changed heart leads to generous action.
slides.notes: Retell Luke 19: Zacchaeus climbs a tree, Jesus welcomes him, and he promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment for fraud. Emphasize repentance, restitution, and welcome. Image: Zacchaeus icon reproduced in the curriculum, printed p. 58.

slides.title: Signs that help us remember
body: Blessed water points us toward God’s blessing.
The cross marks our belonging to Christ.
We pray for the living and the departed.
slides.notes: The curriculum connects marked doorposts with Passover in Exodus 12 and recalls God’s protection of Noah and others. Explain these as biblical connections in the prayers, not a guarantee that a household will never face hardship.

slides.title: Keep the blessing alive each day
body: Give thanks together.
Forgive and work through disagreements.
Share what you have with someone in need.
slides.notes: New application grounded in the lesson. Ask students to choose one realistic habit for the coming week. Do not require private family disclosures or suggest children are responsible for solving adult conflict.

slides.title: Chapter 10 quick quiz
body: 1. Why do we ask for a house blessing?
2. How did Zacchaeus show a changed heart?
3. Name one habit of a Christian home.
slides.notes: Pause before the answer slide. These are newly written curriculum-based practice questions. Accept equivalent meaning.

slides.title: Answers and one idea to remember
body: 1. To dedicate our home and life to God.
2. He gave to the poor and promised repayment.
3. Prayer, gratitude, forgiveness, or generosity.
A Christian home lives Christ’s love.
slides.notes: For detail: Zacchaeus promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment for fraud. End by asking for one small, kind action students can practice this week.
